prompt: Reis moves to room B-310 and three rows carry the room. Two of the three are updated. What is this called?
hint: One fact, several places.

choices.text: An update anomaly
choices.why: The database now holds two answers and nothing says which is right.

choices.text: A deletion anomaly
choices.why: That is a fact disappearing when something else is removed.

choices.text: A referential integrity failure
choices.why: Every pointer still points at something real; the trouble is a repeated value.

choices.text: An insertion anomaly
choices.why: That is having nowhere to put a fact until something else exists.

prompt: A new course is created and nobody has enrolled. There is nowhere to record it. Which anomaly?
hint: The row is an enrolment, so a course exists only where one happens.

choices.text: A violation of first normal form
choices.why: Every cell still holds one value.

choices.text: An update anomaly
choices.why: Nothing is being changed here.

choices.text: A deletion anomaly
choices.why: Nothing is being removed here.

choices.text: An insertion anomaly
choices.why: Recording the course means inventing a student, or waiting.

prompt: Ana withdraws from NET200 and the row is deleted. The course itself disappears. What was the underlying cause?
hint: Ask what a row of that table is.

choices.text: A cascade removed rows in another table
choices.why: Nothing cascaded; the fact was inside the row that went.

choices.text: The course lived only beside an enrolment
choices.why: A row is an enrolment, so facts about courses had nowhere else to live.

choices.text: The course had no primary key of its own
choices.why: It had no table of its own, which is the larger problem.

choices.text: The delete was missing a WHERE clause and took too much
choices.why: One row was deleted, and it was the right one.

prompt: What do all four anomalies come from?
hint: One sentence, and it is about what a row is.

choices.text: The rows are not in any particular order
choices.why: Rows never are, in any table.

choices.text: The table has no foreign keys
choices.why: It has no other tables to point at, which is downstream of the cause.

choices.text: The table is about several kinds of thing
choices.why: So facts about each can only live where the others put them.

choices.text: The table has more columns than a row can justify
choices.why: Width decides nothing; a wide table about one thing is fine.

prompt: A split that loses information is not normalisation. The pieces must join back to give the original, which is why the word for what normalisation does is ___.
hint: One word, and it is what splitting a table into several is called.

prompt: What does A determines B mean?
hint: It is about what you can work out from what.

choices.text: Knowing A is enough to know B
choices.why: Give me A and I can tell you B, with no further information.

choices.text: Changing A changes B
choices.why: Sometimes true and not what the arrow says.

choices.text: A and B appear side by side in the table
choices.why: They do, and that is a consequence rather than the meaning.

choices.text: A and B are both part of the key
choices.why: Neither has to be.

prompt: Today every row with SQL101 also shows Reis. How do you decide whether course_code determines teacher?
hint: The rows you have are not the question.

choices.text: Check whether course_code is the primary key
choices.why: Dependencies exist between non-key columns too.

choices.text: Ask whether one course could ever have two teachers
choices.why: A dependency is a fact about the business, not about today's rows.

choices.text: Count how many distinct teachers the table holds
choices.why: A count of what happened says nothing about what may happen.

choices.text: Check whether it holds for the rows stored today
choices.why: Which is how a program would answer, and why a program cannot do this.

prompt: Match each kind of dependency to what makes it that kind.
hint: Two of them are named in a normal form; one is the healthy case.

pairs.right: On the whole key, and on nothing else
On only some of the columns of a composite key
On the key by way of another non-key column

right_distractors: On a column in a different table
On the order the rows were inserted in

prompt: In the enrolments table, grade depends on neither student nor course alone. What does that tell you about where it belongs?
hint: Lesson 1 met this shape under another name.

choices.text: It should be moved to the students table
choices.why: A student has several grades, so it cannot live there.

choices.text: It should be computed from the two sides rather than stored
choices.why: Nothing derives a grade; somebody records it.

choices.text: It should be split into two columns
choices.why: One grade is one value about one pair.

choices.text: It is a fact about the pairing
choices.why: Which is why it is the one column that survives every split ahead.

prompt: A column holds 'SQL101, NET200'. Which problem is NOT solved by splitting it into rows?
hint: Three of these are cured by the split. One is about something else entirely.

choices.text: Two enrolments in the same second losing one
choices.why: An INSERT cannot lose another; a read-append-write can.

choices.text: Deciding which courses to offer
choices.why: A business question the shape of a table has no bearing on.

choices.text: Searching for SQL101 also matching SQL1010
choices.why: Whole values compare as whole values once each is its own row.

choices.text: No guarantee that NET200 is a real course
choices.why: A REFERENCES cannot be declared on a fragment of a string.

prompt: A table with columns course_1, grade_1, course_2, grade_2, course_3, grade_3. What is wrong?
hint: Ask what a student taking a fourth course would cost.

choices.text: Three courses is too few for most students
choices.why: A limit worth questioning, and not what makes the shape wrong.

choices.text: Integers and text should not share a table
choices.why: They share tables constantly and always have.

choices.text: The columns are not in alphabetical order
choices.why: Column order is presentation and decides nothing.

choices.text: A fourth course would need an ALTER TABLE
choices.why: Data grows in rows; structure grows in columns.

prompt: Is a full name in one column a breach of first normal form?
hint: Everything can be divided. That is not the question.

choices.text: It depends on whether anything needs the parts
choices.why: Sort by surname and it is two facts; only ever print it and it is one.

choices.text: Yes, when the column is part of the key
choices.why: The key does not change what a value is.

choices.text: Yes, because a name is made of two words
choices.why: By that reasoning no text column would ever be legal.

choices.text: No, because text is one type and one value
choices.why: Type has nothing to do with whether the value is one value.

prompt: When is a jsonb or array column a reasonable choice rather than a table?
hint: It is about what you will want to ask.

choices.text: For any list of fewer than about ten items
choices.why: Length is not the criterion at all.

choices.text: For an opaque payload nothing asks about
choices.why: And the cost is named rather than hidden: no foreign key into an element.

choices.text: When the values happen to share a type
choices.why: Being uniform is what makes a table easy, not what makes an array right.

choices.text: Whenever it would save writing a join
choices.why: Which is the reasoning that produces a schema nothing can be asked of.

prompt: Splitting a list out of a cell produces a third table keyed by the pair. Lesson 1 already had a name for that table: a ___ table.
hint: One word, and it sits between the two things it relates.

prompt: Key is (student_email, course_code). student_name depends on student_email alone. What is that?
hint: It depends on some of the key.

choices.text: A violation of first normal form
choices.why: Every cell still holds one value.

choices.text: A transitive dependency, which third normal form removes
choices.why: That one goes through a non-key column.

choices.text: A full dependency, which is healthy
choices.why: A full one needs all of the key.

choices.text: A partial dependency, which second normal form removes
choices.why: The table's rows are finer-grained than the fact is.

prompt: Which tables cannot possibly break second normal form?
hint: Think about what a partial dependency needs in order to exist.

choices.text: Any table already in third normal form
choices.why: 3NF includes 2NF, so this is true and circular rather than the reason.

choices.text: Any table with fewer than five columns
choices.why: Column count has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: Any table whose primary key is a single column
choices.why: There are no parts of the key for a column to depend on.

choices.text: Any table with a generated integer key and no other columns
choices.why: Being generated is not what matters; being one column is.

prompt: Somebody proposes adding a surrogate id to the enrolments table so it satisfies 2NF. What does that achieve?
hint: Ask whether the name is written any fewer times afterwards.

choices.text: Nothing — the name still repeats
choices.why: It hides the dependency on the real identity rather than removing it.

choices.text: It removes the partial dependency correctly
choices.why: The repetition is untouched, which is what the form exists to remove.

choices.text: It makes the table narrower and quicker to scan
choices.why: It adds a column.

choices.text: It removes the need for a foreign key
choices.why: The references are unrelated to the key's shape.

prompt: After splitting students and courses out, which column stayed on enrolments, and why?
hint: One column needed both halves of the key all along.

choices.text: student_name, because it identifies the row
choices.why: It identifies a student, which is why it left.

choices.text: It kept the key alone, so no column stayed
choices.why: It kept its key and its grade.

choices.text: course_title, because it is short
choices.why: Length decides nothing about where a fact belongs.

choices.text: grade, because it depends on the whole key
choices.why: You cannot know it from the student, and you cannot know it from the course.

prompt: code determines teacher, and teacher determines teacher_room. What kind of dependency is code to teacher_room?
hint: It arrives by way of something.

choices.text: Full
choices.why: A full dependency does not pass through anything.

choices.text: Multivalued
choices.why: That is fourth normal form's concern.

choices.text: Partial
choices.why: That needs a composite key, and this key is one column.

choices.text: Transitive
choices.why: The key reaches the room through an ordinary column, which is what 3NF bans.

prompt: After the split, teacher_id still repeats down the courses table. Is that a problem?
hint: There is a difference between repeating a pointer and repeating a fact.

choices.text: Yes, once a teacher has several courses
choices.why: A count does not change whether a value is a pointer.

choices.text: Yes, and it needs another split
choices.why: Splitting a foreign key out would leave nothing pointing at anything.

choices.text: No — repeating a reference is how the model works
choices.why: What 3NF removes is repeating the fact, and the room now lives in one row.

choices.text: Yes, unless the column is indexed
choices.why: An index is about speed and says nothing about redundancy.

prompt: One question replaces all three forms once you can apply it. Which?
hint: It is lesson 1's test, one column at a time.

choices.text: Does this column appear in another table?
choices.why: Pointers appear in several tables by design.

choices.text: Is this a fact about what this row is?
choices.why: Title is about the course; room is about a teacher, so out it goes.

choices.text: Could this column ever be empty?
choices.why: A nullability question, and a different one.

choices.text: Is this column covered by an index already?
choices.why: Speed, not shape.

prompt: A table is in third normal form. What does that NOT tell you?
hint: The forms remove one class of defect.

choices.text: That each column depends on the key in full
choices.why: 2NF is included in 3NF, so this holds too.

choices.text: That the update anomaly from a repeated fact is gone
choices.why: Also exactly what it tells you.

choices.text: That no non-key column depends on another
choices.why: That is exactly what it tells you.

choices.text: That it is a good model of what you are describing
choices.why: Wrong grain, a missing concept and a status that should be a table all survive 3NF.

prompt: Complete the sentence that carries all three forms: every non-key column depends on the key, the ___ key, and nothing ___ the key.
hint: Two words. The first is 2NF and the second opens 3NF.

prompt: Through three decompositions, grade never moved. What does that show?
hint: It depended on the whole key from the first moment.

choices.text: Normalisation leaves integer columns alone
choices.why: Type has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: A well-placed fact has nowhere else to go
choices.why: Which is what you are aiming at: every column somewhere nobody could argue with.

choices.text: Grades matter too little to the model to move
choices.why: They are the one thing the enrolments table is for.

choices.text: It should have been moved and was overlooked
choices.why: It is on the table whose key it depends on, which is where it belongs.

prompt: Put the decomposition in the order it happened.
hint: You cannot pull a teacher out of a courses table that does not exist yet.
items: One table, with courses and grades as lists in cells
Each list value becomes its own row, keyed by the pair
Students and courses leave, because they depended on half the key
Teachers leave courses, because the room was a fact about them
trap: The common swap is doing 2NF before 1NF — a partial dependency cannot be seen while a cell still holds a list, because the key is not yet what it will be.

prompt: In practice, what are the normal forms most useful for?
hint: Think about two people disagreeing about a table.

choices.text: Arguing precisely, and reading inherited schemas
choices.why: That a transitive dependency exists is a claim; it feels cleaner is not.

choices.text: Proving a schema has no bugs
choices.why: They remove one class of defect and say nothing about the rest.

choices.text: Deciding which of a table's columns to index
choices.why: A different subject entirely.

choices.text: Producing a schema from scratch, step by step
choices.why: Nobody builds in 0NF and normalises three times.

prompt: What does BCNF close that third normal form leaves open?
hint: 3NF only constrains what non-key columns may depend on.

choices.text: A cell holding several values at once
choices.why: That is first.

choices.text: A non-key column determining part of a key
choices.why: 3NF says nothing about that direction, and the anomaly is real.

choices.text: A table that needs three pieces to reconstruct
choices.why: That is fifth.

choices.text: Two independent multivalued facts in one table
choices.why: That is fourth normal form.

prompt: Why is third normal form the working standard rather than the fifth?
hint: Weigh what each buys against what each costs.

choices.text: The anomalies are gone, and each split costs a join
choices.why: Everything past it handles shapes that are unusual.

choices.text: Few databases can express the higher forms
choices.why: Nothing in SQL prevents any of them.

choices.text: The higher forms have been shown to be unsound
choices.why: They are sound; they are rare.

choices.text: The fifth form requires a feature PostgreSQL lacks
choices.why: Normal forms are design properties, not features.

prompt: What is being traded when you denormalise?
hint: One side of the trade is guaranteed and the other is measured.

choices.text: A guaranteed property for a measured one
choices.why: And the trade is only honest if the measurement is real.

choices.text: Standards compliance for practicality
choices.why: No standard forbids it.

choices.text: Storage on disk for speed on reads
choices.why: Storage is the cheapest thing in the exchange and never the point.

choices.text: Readability for speed
choices.why: The query gets shorter, which is the opposite of a cost.

prompt: Of the four gates before denormalising, which one do people skip?
hint: It is about the future rather than about today's query.

choices.text: Checking the query is slow in production
choices.why: Skipped sometimes, and the one people at least think about.

choices.text: Rewriting the query into a single statement
choices.why: Also tried, usually before anybody proposes a schema change.

choices.text: Knowing what will keep the copy correct
choices.why: Without one it is not an optimisation, it is a bug with a schedule.

choices.text: Trying an index first
choices.why: Frequently skipped, and it is the second gate rather than the forgotten one.

prompt: What makes a nightly reporting table safe to be redundant?
hint: Ask what would happen if it were wrong.

choices.text: It is rebuilt by a job and never written by hand
choices.why: Being rebuilt is what makes the redundancy repairable rather than a second truth.

choices.text: The application may read it and not write it
choices.why: Read-only and stale is still stale.

choices.text: It lives in a database of its own, far away
choices.why: Location does not make a copy correct.

choices.text: It holds aggregates rather than raw rows
choices.why: Aggregates drift exactly like anything else.

prompt: A comment_count column is added and the application increments it. What is the specific risk?
hint: Count the routes that can create or remove a comment.

choices.text: A forgotten route writes one and the count drifts
choices.why: One mechanism is the requirement; the application is several mechanisms wearing one name.

choices.text: The increment is slower than counting
choices.why: It is faster, which is why it was proposed.

choices.text: Indexing the column turns out to be impossible
choices.why: It can, and that is unrelated.

choices.text: Counting would have returned a different type
choices.why: Both are integers.

prompt: The order, in three words: normalise first, ___, then denormalise only the thing that word pointed at.
hint: One word, and it is what separates a decision from a reflex.

prompt: The one question that separates a snapshot from a copy is:
hint: It is about what should happen next, not about what is stored now.

choices.text: Is this value stored in more than one table?
choices.why: Both cases are, which is why the question cannot be this.

choices.text: Was this value computed, or entered by a person?
choices.why: Either can be either.

choices.text: If the source changes, should this?
choices.why: No means snapshot. Yes means copy.

choices.text: Is this value ever updated?
choices.why: Snapshots are not, and neither are plenty of copies.

prompt: Why is storing only products.price, and reading it for old orders, worse than it looks?
hint: Think about what happens to March once April arrives.

choices.text: It makes the query slower on an old order
choices.why: One fewer column is not slower.

choices.text: It drops the table back to second normal form
choices.why: Normal forms are not what is at stake.

choices.text: It destroys information
choices.why: The invoice printed in March stops matching the database in April.

choices.text: It breaks the foreign key to products
choices.why: The reference is untouched.

prompt: Which of these should be stored as a snapshot rather than read live? Choose all that apply.
hint: Apply the one question to each: if the source changes, should this change too?

choices.text: The delivery address an order was actually sent to
choices.why: The customer moved; the parcel still went to the old address.

choices.text: The room a teacher currently works in
choices.why: If she moves, every course should say the new room. That was a copy, and it went.

choices.text: The exchange rate applied to a payment
choices.why: Rates move constantly and the payment happened once.

choices.text: The tax rate that was charged on an invoice
choices.why: The rate changed; what was charged did not.

prompt: Somebody says we denormalised the price onto the order line. What is the right response?
hint: Ask whether the two columns hold the same fact.

choices.text: They need a trigger to keep the two in step
choices.why: Keeping them in step is precisely what must not happen.

choices.text: They should measure before doing that
choices.why: Sound advice about a decision that is not being made here.

choices.text: They should store the product id instead
choices.why: It already does, beside the price it charged.

choices.text: They did not — they modelled it correctly
choices.why: What this costs and what this cost that day are independent facts.

prompt: Getting the snapshot decision wrong produces which kind of failure?
hint: Does anybody see an error?

choices.text: A silent correctness one
choices.why: Nobody gets an error; the numbers just stop being what they were.

choices.text: A crash the moment the source row is deleted
choices.why: The reference holds; the value read is simply the current one.

choices.text: A constraint violation at write time
choices.why: Every write succeeds, which is the problem.

choices.text: A performance one that appears under load
choices.why: Nothing about it is slow.

prompt: Which of these is a fact about the world rather than about a table?
hint: One of them could be checked by a program, and the others could not.

choices.text: Whether two rows share a value today
choices.why: Read the rows and you know.

choices.text: Could a course have two teachers?
choices.why: A dependency is a claim about what may happen, which is why nothing automates it.

choices.text: Whether the table has a primary key declared
choices.why: Read the DDL and you know.

choices.text: Whether a column is currently nullable
choices.why: Read the DDL and you know that too.

prompt: The notation for a dependency is an arrow, and it is read aloud as: A ___ B.
hint: One word, and it is the verb the arrow stands for.

prompt: A partial dependency can exist in which tables?
hint: It needs parts to be a part of.

choices.text: Any table with a foreign key
choices.why: References have nothing to do with the key's shape.

choices.text: Those with a composite key
choices.why: There are no parts of a single-column key.

choices.text: Any table already in first normal form
choices.why: 1NF is required and not sufficient to create the possibility.

choices.text: Any table with a nullable column
choices.why: Nullability is unrelated.

prompt: Removing a partial dependency means giving whatever it depended on a table of its own, keyed by that ___.
hint: One word: what student_email became in the students table.

prompt: The join table appeared at which step?
hint: It arrived with the first split, not the last.

choices.text: It was there from the start, in the original table
choices.why: The original was one row per enrolment with everything on it.

choices.text: At third normal form, with teachers
choices.why: That split touched courses, not enrolments.

choices.text: At second normal form, when students and courses left
choices.why: Those took columns off it; they did not create it.

choices.text: At 1NF, when the list left the cell
choices.why: A list in a cell is a many-to-many somebody tried not to model.

prompt: In the final schema, why did teachers get a generated key while courses kept its code?
hint: Ask which of the two is the kind of thing that changes.

choices.text: A name is too long to be a key
choices.why: Length is not why a natural key fails.

choices.text: Generated keys are required on tables created later
choices.why: Nothing about creation order decides a key.

choices.text: Text keys are not allowed in a table with a foreign key
choices.why: They are, and courses is referenced by code.

choices.text: A name changes; a printed code does not
choices.why: Normalisation says split; which key the new table gets is still your decision.

prompt: In the tutor example, which dependency is the one third normal form fails to catch?
hint: Look at what is on each side of the arrow.

choices.text: subject determines tutor
choices.why: Several tutors teach the same subject.

choices.text: student determines tutor
choices.why: It does not; a student has a tutor per subject.

choices.text: student and subject together determine tutor
choices.why: That is the healthy full dependency on the key.

choices.text: tutor determines subject, a key column
choices.why: 3NF constrains what non-key columns depend on, not what they determine.

prompt: Three textbooks and four scheduled times for one course, in one table. What do you get?
hint: The two lists have nothing to do with each other.

choices.text: A violation of first normal form
choices.why: Every cell still holds one value.

choices.text: Twelve rows saying nothing
choices.why: The multiplying of unrelated things is the symptom fourth normal form names.

choices.text: Seven rows, one per item
choices.why: Only if the table were already two tables, which is the fix.

choices.text: A transitive dependency through the course
choices.why: Neither list determines the other.

prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the four anomalies the lesson names?
hint: Three are about facts in the wrong place. One is about something else.

choices.text: Having nowhere to record a course with no enrolments
choices.why: The insertion anomaly.

choices.text: One fact repeated so the copies can disagree
choices.why: The update anomaly, by another name.

choices.text: Rows coming back in an odd order
choices.why: Rows have no order in any table, normalised or not.

choices.text: A course vanishing when an enrolment is removed
choices.why: The deletion anomaly.

prompt: Two parallel lists, courses and grades, matched by position. What is the failure mode?
hint: Insert something into one of them.

choices.text: The lists can hold different types
choices.why: They can, and that is a separate problem.

choices.text: One insert shifts every later grade
choices.why: Nothing joins by position safely, and nothing complains when it breaks.

choices.text: Neither list can be sorted
choices.why: Sorting them would be the fastest way to destroy the pairing, which is the same defect.

choices.text: The lists take more space than columns would
choices.why: Space is not the issue anywhere in this lesson.

prompt: What is usually behind a complaint that a join is slow?
hint: Two lessons ahead answer this, and one of them is not about the schema.

choices.text: The database being on another machine
choices.why: A real cost, and not the usual one.

choices.text: Too many tables in the schema
choices.why: Table count does not decide query cost.

choices.text: Third normal form itself
choices.why: The form is not a performance property.

choices.text: A missing index on the foreign key
choices.why: An index is a change nobody has to remember afterwards.

prompt: This repository captures a certificate's title at issue rather than reading it live. Why?
hint: Ask what a renamed course would do to a document somebody already holds.

choices.text: Read live, it would name something else
choices.why: A course can be renamed or removed, and the document says what it said.

choices.text: Certificates are issued before the course exists
choices.why: They are issued after it has been studied.

choices.text: The catalogue is in another database
choices.why: It is in the same one.

choices.text: Reading it live would be slower to render
choices.why: Speed is not what is at stake in a document.

prompt: A support system has one table: `tickets (ticket_id PRIMARY KEY, customer_email, customer_name, agent, agent_team, opened_on)`. Which is the first normal form it breaks?
hint: Check what each form needs in order to be breakable at all.

choices.text: First, because a ticket holds several facts
choices.why: First normal form is about several values in one cell, not several facts in one row.

choices.text: Second, because the name belongs to the customer
choices.why: Second normal form can only be broken by a key with parts, and this key is one column.

choices.text: Third, because ordinary columns determine other ordinary columns
choices.why: The email determines the name and the agent determines the team, both by way of a column that is not the key.

choices.text: None; it is in third normal form and merely wide
choices.why: Move an agent to another team and several rows have to change together.

prompt: A payroll system stores `tax_rate` on every payslip, and also keeps the current rate in a `tax_rates` table. The government raises the rate in July. Should the payslips issued in June change?
hint: Say the two facts out loud, one after the other.

choices.text: No, so the rate on the payslip is a snapshot and belongs there
choices.why: What was charged is a fact about June and does not move when the rate does.

choices.text: Yes, so the rate on the payslip is a copy and should be removed
choices.why: Then last year's payslips would silently re-compute themselves every time a rate changed.

choices.text: No, but the payslip should join and filter by date instead
choices.why: That works only while every past rate is kept and nobody ever edits one.

choices.text: Yes, because one fact must never be stored twice
choices.why: These are two facts: what the rate is, and what was applied on a day.

prompt: A podcast app stores `show_name` on every episode row, next to a `shows` table that holds the name too. A show is renamed. What is the right reading?
hint: Ask whether the stored value should follow the source.

choices.text: A snapshot, like the price on an order line
choices.why: An episode does not belong to the old name the way a sale belongs to the day's price.

choices.text: A copy, and it should come out
choices.why: The episode is of the show that was renamed, so the stored name should follow it and can be left behind.

choices.text: Neither; two tables may hold the same text
choices.why: They may hold the same value only when they are two facts. Here it is one.

choices.text: A copy, but keeping it is free because names rarely change
choices.why: Rarely is what makes it expensive: the drift is found long after the rename.

prompt: `warehouse_stock (sku, warehouse_code, warehouse_city, quantity)` has the key `(sku, warehouse_code)`. What is wrong, and what does the fix produce?
hint: Ask what each column needs in order to be known.

choices.text: Nothing; the city describes where the stock is
choices.why: It describes where the warehouse is, and it is written once per product held there.

choices.text: `quantity` depends on part of the key; move it to a table of its own
choices.why: The quantity is the one column that needs both halves. It is exactly where it belongs.

choices.text: `warehouse_city` depends on half the key; a `warehouses` table appears
choices.why: A partial dependency, so the city moves to a table keyed by the warehouse.

choices.text: The key should be a generated id, which settles it
choices.why: That hides the dependency. The city would still be written once per product.

prompt: A clinic copies the patient's phone number onto every appointment at the moment it is booked, so staff can call them. The patient later changes their number. Is the copied number a snapshot?
hint: Ask what the number is there to do.

choices.text: Yes, because it records the number as it was on the day
choices.why: Nothing needs that. Nobody will ever want to ring the number the patient used to have.

choices.text: No, because the clinic should ring the number they have now
choices.why: The stored value should follow the source, which makes it a copy and an anomaly waiting.

choices.text: Yes, because the appointment happened at a moment
choices.why: The appointment did. The phone number is not a fact about that moment.

choices.text: No, and the fix is to copy it again whenever it changes
choices.why: That is the mechanism problem, and it is the reason to keep one copy rather than many.

prompt: A stored `comment_count` is maintained by a trigger, and also by a nightly job that recounts and repairs it. Why is having both worse than having one?
hint: Ask what happens on the day the two produce different numbers.

choices.text: The nightly job is slower than the trigger
choices.why: It is, and that is a cost rather than the defect.

choices.text: Two mechanisms is the state in which they disagree
choices.why: When the number is wrong, nothing says which of the two was meant to be right.

choices.text: Triggers cannot count rows in another table
choices.why: They can. That is what makes them a workable mechanism here.

choices.text: A count that can be recomputed should never be stored
choices.why: Being recomputable is what makes it checkable, and it is a point in its favour.

prompt: `teacher_id` runs 1, 2, 1, 1 down the `courses` table after the whole decomposition. When is a value repeated down a column fine?
hint: Two things can repeat, and only one of them can disagree with itself.

choices.text: When it is a pointer rather than a copy of a fact
choices.why: Every row points at the one place the fact lives, so there is nothing to fall out of step.

choices.text: When the table is small enough for it not to matter
choices.why: Size decides nothing here; the same table at ten million rows is equally fine.

choices.text: When the column is indexed
choices.why: An index is about finding rows and says nothing about where a fact is stored.

choices.text: When nobody has complained about it yet
choices.why: That is how the anomalies get in, not a reason they are absent.

prompt: A driving school: a pupil has one instructor per licence category, and each instructor teaches only one category. One table holds `(pupil, category, instructor)`. Which dependency is the one the third normal form does not catch?
hint: Look at which side of each arrow is part of the key.

choices.text: `pupil, category → instructor`
choices.why: That one is from the whole key, which is the healthy case.

choices.text: `instructor → category`
choices.why: An ordinary column determining a key column, which third normal form says nothing about and the fourth rule of Boyce and Codd does.

choices.text: `pupil → category`
choices.why: A pupil may take more than one category, so that is not a dependency at all.

choices.text: `category → instructor`
choices.why: A category has many instructors, so knowing it tells you nothing about which.

prompt: A `shipments` table stores the destination address copied from the customer at dispatch. The customer moves, and somebody updates the old shipments to the new address. What did that destroy?
hint: Ask what those rows were the record of.

choices.text: Nothing; the address is now correct everywhere
choices.why: It is now the same in every row and wrong in most of them.

choices.text: The record of where each parcel was actually sent
choices.why: The address on a shipment is a fact about that dispatch, and there is nothing left to recover it from.

choices.text: The foreign key to the customer
choices.why: That is untouched. The pointer was never the problem.

choices.text: The index on the address column
choices.why: An update maintains its indexes; nothing about them is lost.

prompt: The key determines the agent, and the agent determines the team, so the key reaches the team by way of an ordinary column. Write the one word for that kind of dependency.
hint: It names the step in the middle.

prompt: A table whose primary key is one generated id cannot break one of the three normal forms, whatever its columns hold. Write that form's number.
hint: It is the one defined against the parts of a key.

prompt: Somebody proposes storing a total that could be summed. Put the four gates in the order they should be tried.
hint: Three of them might mean you never denormalise at all.
items: Establish that the query is slow on production-sized data
Try an index on the foreign key
Decide what mechanism will keep the stored value true
trap: The gate people skip is the last one, and it is the one that turns a stored total into a bug with a schedule.
